books.blurb: A whole course on the Saṅgaha by a Myanmar Abhidhamma teacher: the nine chapters explained with tables, symbols and reviews, from the 89 cittas to the stages of insight.
books.note: The whole book, one chapter per page: the Preface and Introduction, the nine chapters, which are the Saṅgaha’s own (each linked to the same chapter in the other books on the Saṅgaha map), and the Conclusion. The charts at the back of the printed book are not in the PDF.

books.note: Volumes I and II, one chapter per page: Volume I has the Introduction and Chapters One to Three (of Three only feeling, roots and functions); Volume II has Chapters Four to Six. books.title: Characteristic, Function, Manifestation & Proximate Cause
books.author: (compiler not named)
books.by: Lakkhaṇa-rasa-paccupaṭṭhāna-padaṭṭhāna · study notes from the commentaries (DhsA, Vism); the compiler is not named
books.blurb: Every ultimate reality defined by its four devices — characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause — in English with the Pāli of the commentaries beside it: the 28 rūpas, the types of consciousness, feeling, perception and the 52 cetasikas.
books.note: The whole document, one aggregate per page: matter (28), consciousness, feeling, perception and formations (the cetasikas, by their groups). books.title: Fundamental Abhidhamma, Parts I–II
books.author: Dr. Nandamālābhivaṃsa
books.edition: Centre for Buddhist Studies, Sagaing, 2nd ed. 2005
books.by: Dr. Ashin Nandamālābhivaṃsa, Sagaing Hills · Centre for Buddhist Studies (CBS), Mahāsubodhayon Monastery, Sagaing, Myanmar
books.blurb: A compact course from a Sagaing teacher, in tables: the history of the Abhidhamma, citta, cetasika, rūpa, the miscellaneous section and the cognitive process (Part I); the mental process again in full, the process-free, causality, meditation and the compendium of categories, with colour charts (Part II).
books.note: One chapter per page. Part I: the Editorial Preface, About the Author and The History of Abhidhamma, then its five chapters — 1 Citta, 2 Cetasika, 3 Rūpa (the Saṅgaha’s chapter VI), 4 Pakiṇṇaka (III), 5 Vīthi (IV). Part II begins again with Chapter 5 Vīthi in a new, longer wording, then 6 Vīthimutta (V), 7 Paccaya (VIII), 8 Kammaṭṭhāna (IX), 9 Samuccaya (VII), and the colour charts that close the book. The Saṅgaha map links each chapter to the Saṅgaha’s chapter. Part II was proofread from a scan; the book’s own misprints are kept.
books.toc_foot: Part I: five chapters, with the history of the Abhidhamma. Part II: Chapters 5–9 and the charts.
books.source: Source: Dr. Nandamālābhivaṃsa, Fundamental Abhidhamma, 2nd extended edition, January 2005, revised November 2005, © Centre for Buddhist Studies, Sagaing. Part I from the PDF (Acrobat from Word, 2006), taken from its text layer; the tables are kept with their columns. Part II from a second copy (247 pages) whose text layer is unreadable: every page was read with OCR and proofread line by line against the page image for this library, the Pāli written from the image; the colour charts at the end are shown as images of the pages, with their text. The book’s misprints are kept as printed.
books.desc: Dr. Nandamālābhivaṃsa’s Fundamental Abhidhamma, Parts I–II: citta, cetasika, rūpa, the miscellaneous section, the mental process, the process-free, causality, meditation and the categories.

books.title: Process of Consciousness and Matter
books.author: Bhaddanta Dr. Rewata Dhamma
books.edition: Triple Gem Publications, 2004 (© 2007 Birmingham Buddhist Vihara); edited by Ven. Dr. Kumarabhivamsa
books.by: (Aggamahāpaṇḍita) Bhaddanta Dr. Rewata Dhamma · edited by (Aggamahāpaṇḍita) Ven. Dr. Kumarabhivamsa · Triple Gem Publications, 2004
books.blurb: A supplement to the Comprehensive Manual on the process of consciousness and matter: citta and cetasikas, the five-door and mind-door processes, absorption, path, fruition, cessation and dying, and the kalāpas of matter, with the processes drawn mind-moment by mind-moment.
books.note: The whole book: the Preface, Acknowledgement and biography, the Introduction, its five chapters, the eight tables of kalāpas, the Notes, Bibliography, Pāli-English Glossary and Index. The book’s page numbers are kept in the margin (and can be reached as #pg113 or #p113, so a chart’s “PCM p113” can be found; the Go to box takes a page number); the index links to them. The notes are endnotes numbered by chapter: each reference opens its note in the Notes. The Saṅgaha map links Chapter I to the Saṅgaha’s chapter I, Chapters II–IV to chapter IV and Chapter V to chapter VI. The book’s own misprints are kept as printed.
books.toc_foot: Five chapters, with the Introduction, the tables, the notes, the glossary and the index.
books.source: Source: Bhaddanta Dr. Rewata Dhamma, Process of Consciousness and Matter, edited by Ven. Dr. Kumarabhivamsa, Triple Gem Publications, 2004, © 2007 Birmingham Buddhist Vihara, printed in Malaysia by arrangement with Sukhi Hotu; sponsored “for free distribution” (the sponsors’ acknowledgement, p. 200). The text is unchanged; the paragraph numbers and the Myanmar edition’s page numbers are as in the file. In Chapter IV the file numbers its paragraphs 1, 2, 4 (there is no 3); the numbers are kept as they are.

books.blurb: The Saṅgaha section by section: Nārada’s Pāli, his English, and his explanatory notes, with diagrams.

Chapters I–VII and IX are the web edition; Chapter VIII, missing from it, is transcribed for this library from the 1956–57 edition (Buddha Sāsana Council reprint, Rangoon, 1970), with its two diagrams.

books.source: Source: Nārada Thera, Abhidhammattha-Sangaha of Anuruddhācariya: A Manual of Abhidhamma, Vājirārāma, Colombo. Chapters I–VII and IX from the web edition of palikanon.com as a PDF (Word, 2010; “for free distribution only”), taken as it is; its Pāli writes plain m and n for ṃ and ṅ, and its diagrams are text tables shown with their columns. Chapter VIII, which that edition lacks, is transcribed from the page images of the first edition (1956–57) as reprinted by the Buddha Sāsana Council, Kaba-Aye, Rangoon, 1970 (pp. 73–103), read against the OCR word by word; its Pāli keeps the print’s diacritics (ṁ written ṃ), and its misprints are kept as printed.
